before: The rule of zero: when standard owning members already manage resources, avoid defining custom destructors, copy operations or move operations just to repeat that work.

Notebook contains a std::string and std::vector. Their generated memberwise copy gives an independent name and vector. A struct makes members public by default; braces supply members in declaration order.

Rule of zero is a design preference, not a ban on destructors. A class directly managing a special handle needs deliberate ownership design. Merely adding a destructor can also affect automatic move generation.

Expected output or behavior: 2 3
. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Add a string note member and verify that copying then editing the copy preserves the original. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: The rule of zero means relying on members that already handle their own resources. You then need zero custom functions just to repeat their copying, moving, or cleanup work.
Notebook contains a string and a vector. The compiler's generated copy copies each member. Here that gives the new Notebook its own name and its own vector of page numbers.
std::string and std::vector already release their storage when destroyed. Notebook does not need a custom destructor to repeat that cleanup.
The program prints 2 3. a keeps its two page numbers. b has its own vector, which grows to three items.

The rule of zero is a useful design choice, not a ban on custom cleanup. A class that directly owns a special resource may need its own design. Writing a destructor can also stop the compiler from generating move operations automatically.

before.question: Make b a Notebook& alias. How do the reported sizes change?
before.explanation: An alias does not copy the member vector. push_back then changes the single original Notebook.

after.question: Declare b as Notebook& b = a instead. What sizes print after push_back?
after.explanation: b is now another name for a. There is one Notebook, and its vector grows to three items.
